body:
_Migrated from issue #1349, filed 2026-08-04._

Found during the v4.1.29 pre-tag gate. Not a release blocker — the code under test is
untouched by that release — but it will keep costing triage time until it's fixed.

## Symptom

`tests/unit/test_1094_failed_conversion_imports_original.py::TestConversionDeadline::test_convert_book_passes_the_deadline_to_the_converter`
fails on a loaded machine:

```
assert captured.get("timeout") == pytest.approx(1234, abs=60)
E   assert 1056.28346079099 == 1234 ± 60
```

It passes in isolation (2.87s). It failed inside a full `-n auto` run while five other
agents were also working the repo.

## Root cause

The converter is handed *what is left* of the budget — `1234 − elapsed` — which is correct
behaviour and the point of the test. But the assertion pins that against a fixed ±60s
tolerance, and the test's own comment states the assumption out loud:

```python
# The converter receives what is LEFT of the budget, not the raw total,
# so two stages can't each spend the whole thing. In a unit test almost
# nothing has elapsed, so it lands just under the total.
```

"Almost nothing has elapsed" is an assumption about the *runner*, not about the code. Under
load ~178s elapsed during setup, so the assertion measured the machine rather than the
behaviour it means to pin. The suite is a heavy one — `test_workflow_safety_invariants.py`
alone has several tests spawning git at 5–51s each — so this is reachable in normal CI too,
not just when agents are running.

## Fix direction

Freeze or inject the clock rather than tolerating it: monkeypatch the time source the
deadline math reads, assert the exact remaining budget, and keep the existing
`timeout <= 1234` check as the invariant that actually matters. That makes it red for the
right reason — a converter handed the *raw* total would still fail — while making it
independent of how busy the machine is.

## Why file it rather than widen the tolerance

Widening ±60 to ±300 would mute the assertion without fixing the class: the test would then
pass on a machine where the budget was genuinely being mis-computed by minutes. Same class
as the ambient-state assertions we've been burned by before — a test that silently changes
meaning depending on the environment it runs in.
title: test_1094 conversion-deadline test asserts against ambient wall-clock, flakes under load
